sections.heading: Prysm Client Updates
sections.summary: Prysm's partial columns PR for Gloas is ready to merge; peer scoring overhaul tested on Hoodi for a week with no regressions.
sections.body:
- Prysm's PR for partial columns for Gloas ([PR #17348](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/prysm/pull/17348)) is fully reviewed, fully tested, and waiting on one dependency PR before merging to the release branch.
- Prysm's peer scoring system overhaul ([design doc](https://hackmd.io/@aarshshah/rkZTUeVdGe), [PR #17410](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/prysm/pull/17410)) is dev complete.
  - Tested on a Hoodi node with many validators for a week with no noticeable regressions.
  - Changes how Prysm ranks peers for pruning when at max connections.
  - Adds significant observability: metrics and RPC APIs showing why peers are disconnected, blacklisted, or graylisted, including gossip rejections by topic and invalid RPC responses filterable by agent (e.g., Lighthouse peers, Teku peers).
  - Internal review starting the next day; will be merged to release branch after review.

sections.heading: Lighthouse and Other Client Updates
sections.summary: Lighthouse fixed incorrectly ordered group ID fields and is working on Waggle attestation broadcast; Nethermind progressing on IPv6 support.
sections.body:
- Lighthouse fixed the incorrectly ordered fields bug (reported by Prysm/Aarsh); fix is merged into Unstable and should be on DevNet 8 images.
- Lighthouse looking to enable puzzles on all networks soon, with some nuance still outstanding.
- Lighthouse raised on ACDC that the Gloas limit for columns was too high (~8 MB, thousands of columns); this is now being replaced by a dynamic limit based on the highest value in the blob schedule. Other client implementations should adjust accordingly.
- Daniel (Lighthouse) started working on Waggle-based attestation broadcast using Quinn's proposal.
- Teku: No specific updates available; Anton (Grandine/Teku) mentioned Teku was fixing some vulnerabilities recently.
- Geth (Csaba): Working on peer pool changes, latency-based protected peer pools, and RowDAS/segmented broadcast work—all in progress branches, not yet merged.
- Nethermind: Gossip sub pool implementation is in master for Glamsterdam; currently working on IPv6 support improvements, nearly complete.

sections.heading: RowDAS Proposal (EIP-8371)
sections.summary: RowDAS distributes blob reconstruction duties across supernodes to reduce redundant CPU work by roughly two orders of magnitude.
sections.body:
- RowDAS brings distributed blob reconstruction from earlier 4DAS research to mainnet. It has two objectives:
  - Vertical distribution: Assigns reconstruction duties to specific supernodes rather than having all 2,000+ supernodes redundantly reconstruct every blob.
  - Horizontal distribution: Enables supernodeless reconstruction so the protocol can reconstruct blobs even without data center supernodes.
- Current mainnet has 2,000+ supernodes (high-custody, high-stake, L2 nodes). Each currently reconstructs all blobs independently.
  - One blob recovery costs ~162 ms of CPU time (including KZG proof computation, single-core).
  - At 32 blobs, that is ~5.2 seconds of CPU core time (parallelizable across cores, not wall-clock time).
  - Csaba also achieved ~45 ms per blob with optimizations when not restricted to a single core.
- RowDAS assigns each supernode a "row" duty (128 rows, mapped to blobs) based on node ID. Nodes reconstruct their assigned row first, share results via column distribution, then fall back to reconstructing other rows if needed.
  - Achieves roughly two orders of magnitude reduction in per-node reconstruction CPU usage.
  - Falls back to PeerDAS-equivalent behavior if the network lacks enough row-assigned nodes.
- Simulations run under various scenarios (no supernodes, 10%, 20% supernodes) comparing PeerDAS vs RowDAS on CPU time, completion latency, and bytes sent.
  - Under adversarial conditions, RowDAS degrades to PeerDAS levels but normally provides significant gains.
  - Column-path distribution performance remains comparable to baseline (within a few milliseconds).
- A simpler "duty-sharded PeerDAS" variant was also presented: row assignments only, no row topics. Supernodes coordinate reconstruction duties and share results through existing column topics.
  - Requires improved partial messages implementation but avoids the complexity of row topics.
  - Could serve as a first-stage implementation before full RowDAS.
- Multiple gossip sub / partial messages optimizations were made in Csaba's implementation branch:
  - Changed IHAVE response policies, heartbeat announcement filtering, cross-topic metadata pushing (telling peers about cells they need even when not on the same topic), phase-aware forwarding (push-to-pull transition based on diffusion feedback), and disciplined pull (single-source requests with short timeouts).
  - These optimizations are protocol-level and do not require EIP synchronization.
- Discussion of whether these partial messages changes could inform Waggle implementation; Daniel (Lighthouse) expressed interest in collaborating.
- Csaba committed to providing a more detailed description of each optimization change.

sections.heading: Fast Payload Broadcast Research
sections.summary: Segmenting a 1 MB execution payload into 32 KB chunks and pipelining distribution reduces P99 latency from over 4 seconds to around 1 second.
sections.body:
- Current store-and-forward gossip of a 1 MB execution payload from a 50 Mbit uplink home node results in P99 latency over 4-5 seconds, far exceeding the ~3 second EPBS deadline.
  - Even with 20% fast (1 Gbit) nodes, baseline gossip barely meets the 3-second target.
  - The protocol does not adequately support minimum hardware requirements.
- Segmenting the payload into 32 KB chunks enables pipelining across hops, dramatically reducing latency.
- Three protocol variants tested (all in Csaba's simulation framework):
  - Variant A: Normal gossip sub with segmented messages on a single topic.
  - Variant B: Partial messages with bitmaps.
  - Variant C: Multi-topic (each segment has its own topic, as in DAS).
- All segmented variants achieve ~1 second P99 latency (range 0.9-1.3s), compared to 4+ seconds baseline.
  - Simple segmentation alone (Variant A) already drops latency to ~1.7 seconds.
  - Adding batch publishing drops it to ~1 second.
  - Phase-aware forwarding (push early, announce later) and disciplined pull (request from one source with short rolling-window timeouts) provide further gains.
- Segment verification requires a Merkle commitment root in the builder's bid. Upon receiving the consensus block containing the bid, nodes can verify each chunk's Merkle proof and forward immediately.
- Race condition handling: When segments arrive before the consensus block, a proposed rule prevents pushing segments to peers who haven't confirmed they have the consensus block, reducing buffering requirements and attack surface.
- Erasure coding was tested and provides additional tail-latency improvement by removing the need for every specific segment.
  - Compression should be applied before segmentation/coding to avoid unbalanced segment sizes.
  - EC is presented as optional—significant gains are achievable without it.
- Csaba noted many performance differences between variants A, B, and C are implementation-level rather than fundamental; aligning implementations could align performance.

sections.heading: ethp2p and Segmented Broadcast Alignment
sections.summary: Raul noted extensive overlap between Csaba's segmented broadcast work and existing ethp2p broadcast implementation; called for alignment and offered collaboration.
sections.body:
- Raul stated that much of the push-pull phase transition, chunking, preamble handling, and parameter configuration presented by Csaba is already implemented and benchmarked in ethp2p broadcast.
  - ethp2p broadcast supports a pluggable encoder/decoder; a no-op encoder can be used to chunk without erasure coding.
  - ethp2p uses a two-phase protocol: a diverge phase (stochastic chunk dispatch) and a converge phase (metadata gossip and availability requests), with a configurable local threshold for transition.
- ethp2p dispatch maps each chunk to an independent QUIC stream, enabling:
  - Interruption or rejection of chunks without consuming them in the application (inspect header, dispose of stream).
  - Smarter handling of races when sending a chunk to a peer that simultaneously reports having it.
- Simulations have been run up to 4,000 nodes in shadow simulation.
- A fuzzer continuously exploring the parameter space exists (not yet public, was interrupted when Raul left EF).
- [NetViz tool](https://netviz.ethp2p.dev/) available for visualizing protocol behavior; built with Claude 4.6.
- Raul proposed aligning efforts and offered to onboard anyone wanting to collaborate on ethp2p.
- Csaba agreed on the need for cross-framework comparison and noted that techniques transfer between implementations.
- LambdaClass has a [WIP Rust implementation of ethp2p](https://github.com/lambdaclass/ethp2p-rs).

sections.heading: EIP-8411: Fast Payload Broadcast
sections.summary: A new EIP proposes replacing the execution payload gossip topic with a chunked topic using Merkle proofs; PFI for Hegota to be discussed at ACD.
sections.body:
- [EIP-8411](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/12299) formalizes the segmented payload broadcast approach presented by Csaba.
- Core change: Replace the execution payload topic with an execution payload chunks topic. The execution payload envelope is segmented into 64 chunks (matching PeerDAS column count for future compatibility).
- No erasure coding in the base EIP, left as an open question.
- The payload bid is extended with a `payload_chunks_root` field (Merkle root) so that once a node has the signed bid, it can verify each chunk's Merkle inclusion proof cheaply and forward immediately.
- Chunk structure includes: data, chunk index, Merkle inclusion proof, slot, and BeaconBlock root.
  - The execution payload envelope (not just the payload itself) is segmented, including execution requests and other fields.
  - `BeaconBlockRoot` must be removed from the envelope before chunking since the builder may not know it at chunking time; it is instead attached per-chunk.
- Handling chunks received before the bid: chunks are queued and not propagated until the signed bid (or beacon block containing the bid) is received—same logic as current execution payload handling.
- Optimization strategies (push-pull transition, batching, etc.) are implementation details, not part of the EIP itself, allowing clients to iterate independently.
- The EIP is intended to replace the already-PFI'd "blobs in blocks" proposal for Hegota; ACD discussion on this planned for the next day.
  - EIP deadline has passed; whether it can be PFI'd for Hegota depends on ACD approval.
- Csaba emphasized the bid change is critical: without it, the attack surface increases due to larger buffering requirements and inability to verify segments early.
- Mixed-network operation (some peers supporting segmented broadcast, others not) is possible but adds complexity and is considered a less clean solution than a fork-coordinated rollout.

sections.heading: ethp2p Integration into Clients via Shared QUIC Transport
sections.summary: ethp2p can coexist with libp2p on a single QUIC endpoint by dispatching streams based on ALPN negotiation and first-byte inspection.
sections.body:
- Design targets for ethp2p-libp2p coexistence:
  - Single QUIC transport and endpoint shared between both stacks.
  - Every connection can serve both ethp2p and libp2p streams.
  - Fully backwards compatible: libp2p-only peers notice nothing.
  - Non-invasive for existing CL code; changes contained at the networking layer.
- Current Prysm QUIC setup lets libp2p construct the transport internally. The change requires the application to own the transport and inject it into both stacks.
  - A small patch to go-libp2p is needed (sitting in a branch, not yet PR'd due to version lineage issues).
- Capability discovery uses TLS 1.3 ALPN negotiation:
  - ethp2p ALPN is advertised first for precedence.
  - If both peers support ethp2p, the connection is split into two views (ethp2p view and libp2p view).
  - If only libp2p is negotiated, the raw QUIC connection is handed entirely to libp2p.
- Stream routing/dispatch:
  - Unidirectional streams → known to be ethp2p (libp2p does not support unidirectional streams).
  - Bidirectional streams → first byte is peeked: if it starts with a slash (after the uvarint), it is a libp2p multistream-select stream. The slash character is reserved and cannot appear in ethp2p.
- Connection lifecycle:
  - Closing one side's view leaves the other alive.
  - ethp2p can receive an advisory when the libp2p side closes, and delegate the decision to the application.
  - Connection fully closes only when both views are released.
- Listener lifecycle:
  - Shared transport returns immediate listeners to both stacks but only begins accepting on the underlying QUIC connection when both have attached (prevents races).
  - Closing a listener from either side alone is made illegal; the application controls the shutdown sequence by closing the shared transport first.
  - Re-listen after close is not expected in any known client lifecycle.
- Dial behavior:
  - libp2p dial: handshake, discover capabilities, split connection if ethp2p supported.
  - ethp2p dial: if remote supports ethp2p, split; if not, best-effort offer the connection to libp2p side (dropped if backlogged).
- Future: ideally the transport/handshake should also be shared with the EL. The EL's devp2p QUIC effort uses a different handshake (web transport compatible, certificate exchange on first stream rather than TLS extension), creating compatibility considerations around connection resumption tokens.
- A Prysm branch integrating ethp2p broadcast for Glamsterdam payload broadcast exists and reportedly works on DevNet.

sections.heading: Unified Networking Specs Site
sections.summary: A new site aggregating all Ethereum networking specs from dispersed repos into a single taxonomy is nearly ready for release.
sections.body:
- Ethereum networking specs are currently fragmented across devp2p repo, consensus specs (fork-based incremental format), EIPs, and other sources.
- Raul (aligned with Felix) is building a unified site ([ethp2p/ethp2p repo](https://github.com/ethp2p/ethp2p)) to aggregate all networking specs in one place.
  - Content from external sources is clearly attributed; newer specs (ethp2p, Waggle, Csaba's broadcast work) can be incubated directly in the repo.
- Taxonomy separates protocols from features: e.g., gossip is defined as a protocol, then Ethereum objects reference it with specific topic definitions and flows.
- Filters allow viewing execution-only, consensus-only, or cross-layer content without a hard top-level separation.
- Data availability has a unified page covering all objects regardless of which stack they sit in.
- Third iteration of the taxonomy; expected to be released publicly within the week for community feedback.

sections.heading: ethp2p Advantages over libp2p
sections.summary: ethp2p exposes QUIC-native features like datagrams, zero-RTT, unidirectional streams, and slot-aware session management that libp2p abstracts away.
sections.body:
- ethp2p provides direct access to QUIC features without libp2p's abstraction layer:
  - Datagrams (useful for attestations), unidirectional streams, congestion control stats for smart routing, zero-RTT connection resumption.
  - libp2p has a [PR for datagram streams](https://github.com/libp2p/specs/pull/680) but it has been open for about a year.
- Zero-RTT enables discovering all network peers, saving resumption tokens, and sending messages without re-handshaking—valuable for proposers needing rapid fan-out.
- ethp2p is slot-aware: the application signals slot boundaries, and caches/propagation state are cleared accordingly, avoiding issues like attestation aggregates bleeding across slots.
- Prysm already uses go-libp2p mostly as a transport layer, having built its own peer manager and scoring around libp2p quirks. Gossip sub is heavily specialized for Ethereum's needs.
- Raul argued that time spent adapting libp2p APIs for Ethereum-specific features (which no other libp2p user needs) would be better spent on building the actual reconciliation protocols and networking logic that matters.
- Raul suggested Hegota is far enough out to leave room for ethp2p adoption; Kamil noted no one knows when it will ship.
- Discussion about whether Waggle, ethp2p, or gossip sub should be used for upcoming features (e.g., Sukun attestation protocol, segmented broadcast) remains open.
